passage: Karthik, you asked how I got over my fear of speaking in client meetings. It started with a silly question I asked myself on the metro. I'd been dreading Monday's presentation because in the last one I said "revenue" when I meant "profit," and I was sure the whole room remembered. So I tried to remember other people's slips from that same meeting. Did the manager stumble? Did anyone say a wrong number? I honestly couldn't recall a single one. Not one. And I was there, listening! That's when it clicked: everyone in that room was busy with their own slides, their own worries. So I told myself, Gurpreet, you're allowed to say things imperfectly. On Monday I stumbled twice. Nobody blinked. Afterwards the client asked me the most questions.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet say instead of "profit"?
qa.a: Revenue.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel before Monday's presentation?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt dread, sure the whole room still remembered the revenue slip.

qa.q: What question helped Gurpreet, and why does it work?
qa.a: How much can I remember of other people's slips? Recalling none showed that people are mostly focused on themselves.

qa.q: How did the client respond to Gurpreet's presentation?
qa.a: The client asked the most questions, showing interest rather than noticing the stumbles.

grounding: A young professional tries to recall others' slips, sees that people are mostly self-focused, and gives permission to speak imperfectly.

passage: I'm Siddharth, and I sat next to Arohi at the regional teachers' workshop, so I saw the whole thing. In the morning session she answered a question and mixed up two policy names. A couple of people glanced over. For the next hour she didn't say a word, pressing her pen into her notebook. At tea she asked me something odd: "Do you remember anyone's mistakes from this morning?" I thought about it. The speaker had dropped his notes; someone had called the chairperson by the wrong name. I only remembered because she asked. "Neither do I," she said. "Except mine." She laughed at herself. In the afternoon session she raised her hand four times. One answer was a bit messy. I can't say what she felt, but she didn't stop.

qa.q: How many times did Arohi raise her hand in the afternoon?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What might Arohi's pressing her pen into her notebook suggest?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and tense about mixing up the policy names, feeling everyone had noticed.

qa.q: What question did Arohi use to reassure herself, and why did it work?
qa.a: Whether anyone remembered others' mistakes from the morning; seeing how little people recall of others' slips gave her permission to speak imperfectly.

qa.q: How did Siddharth experience Arohi's question at tea?
qa.a: Siddharth found it odd and could only recall others' slips because she asked, which showed how little people notice.

grounding: A colleague describes a young teacher who checks how little she remembers of others' slips and goes back to speaking up.

passage:
Monday. At the weekly ops meeting, Amandeep, the only woman on the team, misread a delivery figure out loud and had to correct herself. Her face burned. For the rest of the day she replayed it, certain Santosh and the others thought she wasn't sharp enough.
Wednesday. Before Friday's meeting she tried an experiment. She wrote down every mistake she could remember others making in the last month of meetings. After ten minutes her page had one line: "Santosh once said Tuesday instead of Thursday?" She wasn't even sure about that one.
Friday. In the meeting she spoke up three times. The second time she muddled a number again, laughed, said, "Sorry, 4,200, not 2,400," and kept going. At lunch Santosh asked her about the new route plan. He didn't mention the numbers. She suspected he didn't remember them at all.

qa.q: What did Amandeep write on her page on Wednesday?
qa.a: "Santosh once said Tuesday instead of Thursday?"

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel after Monday's meeting?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, face burning, and anxious that the others thought she wasn't sharp enough.

qa.q: What experiment did Amandeep try, and what did it show?
qa.a: Writing down every mistake she remembered others making; she could barely recall one, which showed people are mostly focused on themselves.

qa.q: What did Santosh seem to care about at lunch?
qa.a: Santosh was interested in the new route plan, not in her muddled numbers.

grounding: Over a week, a young professional tests how much she remembers of others' slips and gives herself permission to speak imperfectly.

passage:
Kindergarten teacher's note, Thursday
During snakes and ladders, Chinmay blew on the dice three times and whispered "six, six, six" before every throw. When he got a six, he shouted, "See! My blowing works!" When he got a one, he said Arnab had "looked at it wrong." Arnab tried blowing too and got a two. Chinmay said Arnab "didn't blow properly." I let them mark their throws on a chart for the rest of the week. We will look at it together on Friday.

qa.q: What did Chinmay whisper before every throw?
qa.a: Six, six, six.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay blow on the dice?
qa.a: He felt excited and in charge, believing his blowing could make a six come up.

qa.q: Why is the throw chart a good idea?
qa.a: Marking all the throws together lets the children see, playfully, that blowing doesn't change the numbers.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when told he didn't blow properly?
qa.a: Arnab might feel confused or left out, since he tried the same thing.

grounding: A kindergarten teacher records a young boy who believes blowing on the dice makes a six come.

passage: On the day of the village cricket final, little Sahil sat on the wall beside his sister Sarika, wearing his red cap backwards. "If I keep my fingers crossed the whole time, Chacha's team wins," he announced. He crossed them so tight his knuckles went white. When Chacha hit a four, Sahil shouted, "My fingers did that!" When Chacha got out, Sahil looked at his hands. "I let go for one second to scratch my nose." Sarika hid a smile. "Maybe the bowler was just good."

qa.q: What was Sahil wearing?
qa.a: His red cap, backwards.

qa.q: Why did Sahil keep his fingers crossed so tight?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and in charge, believing his crossed fingers could make Chacha's team win.

qa.q: How could Sarika help Sahil without spoiling his fun?
qa.a: Let him enjoy crossing his fingers, while gently showing that the bowler and batters decide the match, as she began to.

qa.q: What might Sarika feel watching Sahil?
qa.a: Sarika seems amused and fond, hiding a smile at his reasoning.

grounding: A young boy believes keeping his fingers crossed decides a cricket match.

passage: Every Saturday Anders watched his father's football team on TV from the same green cushion, holding his left sock in his hand. "If I hold the sock, they score," he told his friend Abebe. That week the team scored twice. "See?" Anders said, waving the sock. The next Saturday Abebe sat on the green cushion first. The team lost. "You sat on my cushion!" Anders cried. Abebe looked at the cushion, then at the TV. "But I wasn't even playing."

qa.q: What did Anders hold while watching?
qa.a: His left sock.

qa.q: Why did Anders blame Abebe for the loss?
qa.a: He felt upset and believed his cushion and sock made the team score, so losing the cushion seemed to cause the loss.

qa.q: What could Anders's father say to help?
qa.a: Gently explain that the players decide the score, and that watching together is the fun part, wherever they sit.

qa.q: How does Abebe see the cushion?
qa.a: Abebe is puzzled, thinking the players, not the cushion, decide the match.

grounding: A young boy believes his cushion and a sock ritual decide his team's result.

passage: Before every test I use my green pen, the one I got for my birthday. I got full marks in the first spelling test with it, so I knew it was lucky. Last week, on the morning of the maths exam, I couldn't find it. I looked under my bed, in my bag, even in the fridge. I started crying at the school gate, and my stomach felt full of bees. Aditi, who sits next to me, gave me her blue pen. "It writes the same," she said. I was sure I would fail. Then I started the sums and forgot about the pen. I got 18 out of 20. Mummy found the green pen in my raincoat pocket that evening. Now I think the pen isn't lucky. Rajni just knows her tables.

qa.q: What mark did Rajni get in the maths exam?
qa.a: 18 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel at the gate without the green pen?
qa.a: She felt anxious and scared, crying, with her stomach full of bees, sure she would fail without the lucky pen.

qa.q: What could help Rajni before the next test?
qa.a: Remembering that she scored 18 with Aditi's blue pen, so her practice, not the pen, earns the marks.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi to lend her pen?
qa.a: Aditi was kind and calm, simply offering a pen that writes the same.

grounding: A girl recalls believing her green pen made her do well and panicking when it went missing before an exam.

passage:
Swimming coach's note, district trials, Saturday
Hansa (10-12 age group) has a routine before every race: she touches the starting block three times, fixes her cap twice, and always swims in lane four. Today the officials put her in lane two. She went pale, said, "I'll lose now," and her hands shook on the block. Devika, from our club, told her lane two was "just water, same as four." I sat with Hansa for two minutes and asked her to count her breaths, not her touches. She swam and finished second, one second faster than her best. Afterwards she asked me, "So lane four isn't magic?" I told her it was her training that made her fast. We will practise in different lanes this week.

qa.q: Which lane does Hansa always swim in?
qa.a: Lane four.

qa.q: Why did Hansa go pale when put in lane two?
qa.a: She felt anxious and frightened that missing her usual lane meant she would lose.

qa.q: What did the coach do, and what is the plan for the week?
qa.a: Helped her count breaths instead of touches, then planned practice in different lanes so the routine loses its hold.

qa.q: How did Devika try to help?
qa.a: Devika calmly told Hansa that lane two was just water, same as four.

grounding: A swimming coach records a girl who believes her lane and routine decide her races, and panics when they change.

passage:
Saturday
Big match day. I always sit in the third seat on the left on the school bus before a match, because that's where I sat when we won the zonal final. Today Lokesh bhaiya drove me in the car instead because the bus was late. No third seat. I felt sick the whole way. I kept thinking, that's it, we'll lose, and it'll be my fault.
We won. By forty runs. I took two catches.
Now I'm lying here thinking. The seat wasn't there, and we still won. So maybe it was never the seat. Maybe it was the nets practice every evening.
I'm still going to sit there next time. But maybe I won't cry if I can't.
Usha

qa.q: How many catches did Usha take?
qa.a: Two catches.

qa.q: How did Usha feel in the car?
qa.a: Usha felt sick and anxious the whole way, sure the team would lose and it would be Usha's fault.

qa.q: What does Usha start to realise, and how could it help next time?
qa.a: That the win came from nets practice, not the seat, which could ease the panic if the seat isn't there again.

qa.q: Why might Lokesh bhaiya have been puzzled by Usha's mood?
qa.a: Lokesh bhaiya was only giving a lift because the bus was late, not knowing how much the seat mattered to Usha.

grounding: A child's diary shows panic at missing a lucky bus seat before a match, and the win that followed anyway.

passage:
"I'm choosing my own raffle number this time. 27. My birthday."
"Kamal, the numbers are drawn from a pot," said Zubin, his cousin, as they stood at the mela stall. "The pot doesn't know your birthday."
"But if I pick it, it's more likely. Last year the uncle gave me a random one and I lost."
"Everyone lost except one person."
"Exactly. I didn't choose. This time I'm choosing."
"Two hundred tickets. One prize. Your number has the same chance as the uncle's number."
"It feels better, though."
"It feels better. It isn't better."
Kamal paid for ticket 27 anyway, holding it like it was warm. At nine they read out the winner: 143. Kamal stared at his ticket. "Maybe I should've picked 143."
Zubin laughed so hard he had to sit down.

qa.q: How many tickets were there?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel choosing 27 made winning more likely?
qa.a: He felt more in control and hopeful picking his birthday number, so it seemed luckier than a random ticket.

qa.q: What does Zubin point out, and why does it matter?
qa.a: That every number has the same chance in the pot, so choosing a number feels better but doesn't change the odds.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Kamal's reaction to 143?
qa.a: Zubin finds it very funny that Kamal still thinks picking a number would have helped.

grounding: A teenage boy believes choosing his own raffle number improves his odds in a pure draw.

passage: At the Pongal fair last year there was a stall with scratch cards: pay ten rupees, scratch three boxes, win a toy or a phone. I was fifteen and sure I had figured it out. I didn't take the top card like everyone else. I asked for one from the middle of the pile, then one from the bottom, then one that felt warm. I thought choosing carefully gave me an edge. My cousin Keerthana watched me spend my whole hundred rupees of pocket money, one card at a time. I won a plastic whistle. She said, "Hemant, the cards don't know which one you picked." I argued all the way home. Later, in maths, we learned about chance, and I felt my face go hot remembering the warm card.

qa.q: What did Hemant win?
qa.a: A plastic whistle.

qa.q: Why did Hemant choose cards from the middle and bottom of the pile?
qa.a: Hemant felt clever and confident, believing careful choosing gave an edge in a game of pure chance.

qa.q: What would you tell Hemant before the next fair?
qa.a: That picking a particular card doesn't change the odds, so decide beforehand whether to play at all, knowing it is only chance.

qa.q: How did Keerthana see the scratch cards?
qa.a: Keerthana saw clearly that the cards don't know which one is picked, and watched, worried, as the pocket money went.

grounding: A teenager recalls believing that carefully choosing scratch cards improved the odds, and spending all the pocket money.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11, 21 January
Ujjwal came to me this morning, worried about his friend Omkar. Omkar has been spending his lunch money on an online number game that promises big prizes. I spoke with Omkar at lunch. He was calm and confident: he said he always picks numbers from his own "system" of dates, so his odds are better than people who let the app choose. He has lost about two thousand rupees over three weeks but believes he is "close to cracking it." I showed him that each draw is random and that his chosen numbers have exactly the same chance as any others. He went quiet. With his agreement, I called his parents this afternoon, and we will all meet tomorrow. I have also reported the site to the principal.

qa.q: How much has Omkar lost over three weeks?
qa.a: About two thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why does Omkar feel confident about the number game?
qa.a: He feels calm and in control, believing numbers chosen from his own system of dates give better odds than letting the app choose.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Showed Omkar that each draw is random, called his parents the same day with his agreement, and reported the site, so he doesn't face it alone.

qa.q: How was Ujjwal feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: Ujjwal was worried about his friend and cared enough to ask an adult for help.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage boy who believes his own chosen numbers beat a random draw, and the same-day steps taken.

passage: It was 1 a.m., the night before his final-semester exam, and Kamal was still on the betting app. He had a system: after every loss, double the next bet, because "a win has to come, and it'll cover everything." He had lost six in a row. His hands were cold. His exam notes lay unopened on the bed. His sister Mahima, home for the holidays, saw the light under his door and came in. She looked at the screen, then at his face. "Kamal. How much?" He told her. She didn't shout. She closed the laptop gently, sat beside him and said, "Tomorrow, after your exam, we talk to Papa, and we call a gambling helpline together. Tonight, you sleep." Kamal wanted to argue about his system. Instead he let her take the laptop to her room.

qa.q: How many losses in a row had Kamal had?
qa.a: Six in a row.

qa.q: Why did Kamal keep doubling his bets?
qa.a: He felt in control and sure his system would bring a win to cover everything, even as his hands went cold with fear.

qa.q: What did Mahima do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, closed the laptop, took it away for the night, and planned to talk to Papa and call a gambling helpline together after the exam.

qa.q: What was it like for Mahima to see the screen?
qa.a: Mahima was probably frightened and worried for Kamal, but chose calm and care over shouting.

grounding: On the night before an exam, a young man doubles his bets believing his system will win it back, and his sister steps in that night.

passage: In the shared flat in Andheri, Tanvir's phone buzzed every few minutes with price alerts. He had started trading with his first salary, and he was sure he had a method: three green candles in a row meant buy, and a red one meant the market was "about to bounce." When a trade went wrong, he put in more to "average down." By March he had lost most of four months' savings. "I just need one good week," he told his flatmate Santosh at dinner. "I'm learning the patterns." Santosh put down his plate. "Tanvir, the price doesn't know your patterns. Every time you lose, you put in more. That's what worries me." Tanvir laughed, but his leg was jiggling under the table. Santosh slid a card across: the number of a certified financial counsellor his cousin had seen.

qa.q: What did Tanvir think three green candles meant?
qa.a: Buy.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir keep putting in more after losses?
qa.a: He feels confident he is learning the patterns and anxious to win the savings back, so putting in more feels like control.

qa.q: What does Santosh do that could help?
qa.a: He names his worry about Tanvir adding money after every loss and passes on a certified financial counsellor's number.

qa.q: How does Santosh seem to feel about Tanvir's trading?
qa.a: Santosh is worried, noticing the losses and the nervous jiggling leg under the laugh.

grounding: A young man believes his trading method can beat random price moves and keeps adding money after losses, while a flatmate voices concern.

passage:
"I lost again. But tonight's different. I've studied every player's last ten innings."
"Omkar, that's what you said on Sunday."
"On Sunday the pitch was weird. That was bad luck. My method is solid."
"How much have you put in this month?"
"Doesn't matter. I'll win it back tonight. I'm doubling the stake."
Rehana put her phone down. "You've doubled it three times already."
"Because I'm close. I can feel it."
"Rain, a dropped catch, one bad over. You can't study those."
"You don't understand the game."
"I understand you haven't eaten dinner and you've been checking your phone since six." She pulled her chair closer. "Can we talk to the college counsellor tomorrow? I'll come with you. Just one talk."
Omkar stared at the screen, thumb hovering over the button, for a long time.

qa.q: How many times has Omkar already doubled the stake?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Omkar feel tonight will be different?
qa.a: He feels confident and close to winning, believing his study of players' innings gives him control over outcomes that are really random.

qa.q: What does Rehana suggest, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Talking to the college counsellor tomorrow with her beside him, getting real help instead of arguing about his method.

qa.q: What does Rehana notice about Omkar's evening?
qa.a: She notices he hasn't eaten and has been checking his phone since six, which worries her.

grounding: A young man believes his study of players gives him an edge in betting and keeps doubling his stake after losses.

passage: Two days before the Christmas plant sale, a hailstorm shredded half of Elizabeth's poinsettias in the greenhouse at her small nursery near Shillong. Her assistant, Aparna, was close to tears. "Maybe it's bad luck from moving the pots last week." Elizabeth sat on an upturned crate and took out a notebook. "Let's split it. What did we control? The greenhouse roof, the watering, the prices, the stall. What didn't we control? The hail." She wrote two columns. The roof panels had been old; she would replace those this month. The rest was weather. "No bad luck from pots," she said gently. "And no blaming ourselves for the sky." They spent the next day potting up the surviving plants and making a sign: HAIL SURVIVORS, EXTRA TOUGH. They sold out by noon.

qa.q: What did the sign say?
qa.a: HAIL SURVIVORS, EXTRA TOUGH.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth seem to feel sitting on the crate?
qa.a: Elizabeth seemed calm and steady, disappointed but focused on sorting what she could and couldn't control.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth separate skill from luck?
qa.a: She wrote two columns, fixing the old roof panels she controlled and accepting the hail as weather, without superstition or self-blame.

qa.q: How was Aparna feeling after the storm?
qa.a: Aparna was close to tears and worried it was bad luck from moving the pots.

grounding: After a hailstorm, a young nursery owner separates what she controlled from what was chance, without superstition or self-blame.

passage: The rejection email arrived on a Tuesday evening in the Hyderabad flat. Vinita read it twice, then sat on the balcony with a cup of tea going cold. Her roommate Farida came out. "Was it the interview dress? You didn't wear your lucky blue one." Vinita smiled a little. "I thought about that too, for a second." Then she took out a notebook and drew a line down the page. On one side: things I controlled. My portfolio, my answers, how I prepared for the case question. On the other: things I didn't. How many people applied, what the panel wanted, whether someone inside was already lined up. She circled one item on the first side: "Case answer, too long." "That I can fix," she said. "The rest isn't a verdict on me." Then she drank the cold tea anyway.

qa.q: What item did Vinita circle?
qa.a: Case answer, too long.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling on the balcony before the notebook?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and flat, letting her tea go cold, and briefly wondered about the lucky dress.

qa.q: What method did Vinita use, and why does it help?
qa.a: Splitting what she controlled from what she didn't, then working on the one fixable item, so she improves without self-blame or superstition.

qa.q: Why might Farida have mentioned the lucky dress?
qa.a: Farida was probably trying to comfort Vinita by finding a simple reason for the rejection.

grounding: After a job rejection, a young woman separates what she controlled from chance and works only on what she can fix.

passage:
"We lost," said Pooja, dropping her file on the chamber table. "Six months of work."
Vidya, her senior, poured two cups of chai. "Tell me what happened, in two lists. What was in your hands?"
"The research. The arguments. The way I handled the witness."
"And what wasn't?"
"Which judge we got. The other side's surprise document. Whether the witness remembered things right."
"Now. On your list, what would you change?"
Pooja thought. "I'd have prepared the witness more on dates. That's on me."
"Good. And the judge?"
"Not on me."
"Right." Vidya handed her a cup. "So you work on witness prep. And you don't rely on your lucky pen next time, or blame yourself for the judge's mood."
Pooja laughed despite herself. "How did you know about the pen?"
"Everyone in this chamber has a pen."

qa.q: What would Pooja change about her own work?
qa.a: She would have prepared the witness more on dates.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she dropped the file on the table?
qa.a: She felt deflated and disappointed after losing six months of work.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Pooja separate skill from luck?
qa.a: By asking for two lists, what was in Pooja's hands and what wasn't, so she works on witness prep and lets go of the judge and the lucky pen.

qa.q: What does Vidya's last line suggest about her own experience?
qa.a: Vidya has seen many lawyers lean on lucky charms, and she gently teases Pooja from experience.

grounding: A young lawyer, guided by her senior, sorts a lost case into what she controlled and what was chance, dropping superstition and self-blame.

passage:
Sunday
Nikita didi and I tossed a coin to decide who gets the TV remote. I always call tails. It was heads. Then heads again. Then heads, heads, heads. FIVE heads in a row! I said, "Okay, the next one HAS to be tails. The coin owes me." Didi laughed and said, "The coin doesn't remember anything." I said that's impossible, it's been heads five times, it has to balance. She tossed. HEADS. Six!
I was so annoyed I went to my room. Then I tossed the coin by myself twenty times and wrote it down. Heads, tails, tails, heads, heads... It was all mixed up. Sometimes three the same. Sometimes not.
Maybe the coin really doesn't remember. That's kind of scary.
Tarun

qa.q: How many heads came in a row in the end?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why was Tarun sure the next toss had to be tails?
qa.a: Tarun felt the coin owed a tails after five heads, as if it would balance itself, and the sixth head left Tarun annoyed.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that helped, and what did it show?
qa.a: Tossed the coin twenty times and wrote down the results, which showed they were mixed and the coin doesn't remember past tosses.

qa.q: How does Nikita didi see the coin?
qa.a: She laughs, knowing the coin doesn't remember anything, so each toss is fresh.

grounding: A child's diary shows certainty that tails must follow five heads, as if chance has a memory.

passage: In the reading room of the village library, Jagdish and Jomon played ludo on the old wooden board every evening. That evening Jagdish hadn't rolled a six in eleven turns, and his last token was stuck at home. "Next one's a six for sure," he said, rattling the dice. "It's been waiting. It's due." "Due?" said Jomon. "The dice doesn't keep a diary." Jagdish rolled. A two. "Okay, NOW it's really due. Twelve turns!" A four. The librarian, Mr Varghese, looked over his glasses. "Jagdish, if I rolled it right now, fresh, what would my chance of a six be?" Jagdish opened his mouth, then frowned. "The same as mine?" "The same as yours on your very first turn, too." Jagdish looked at the dice as if it had tricked him. Then he rolled a six.

qa.q: How many turns had Jagdish gone without a six at first?
qa.a: Eleven turns.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish feel a six was due?
qa.a: He felt impatient and sure the dice would make up for the missing sixes, as if it remembered the long wait.

qa.q: How did Mr Varghese's question help?
qa.a: Asking what the chance would be on a fresh roll showed Jagdish that every roll has the same chance, whatever came before.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the dice?
qa.a: Jomon jokes that the dice doesn't keep a diary, seeing each roll as fresh.

grounding: A boy is sure a six is due after many turns without one, believing the dice remembers.

passage: At the school fair in Nairobi there was a spinning wheel with red and black slices, and every spin cost one token. Jamal watched it land on red four times in a row. "Black is coming," he told his sister Wanjiru. "It has to. Red's had its turn." He put all five of his tokens on black. Red. "That's five reds! Now black is super due." Wanjiru held his arm before he could spend the tokens she had given him for the cake stall. "Jamal, does the wheel know what it did before?" He stopped. The wheel was just painted wood and a pointer. "No..." "So every spin is like the first spin." Jamal looked at his empty hands, then at the cake stall, and let her lead him there.

qa.q: How many tokens did Jamal put on black?
qa.a: All five of his tokens.

qa.q: Why did Jamal believe black was super due?
qa.a: He felt excited and certain the wheel had to balance after so many reds, as if it remembered its turns.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped him spending the cake tokens and asked if the wheel knew what it did before, showing every spin is fresh.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru have felt watching Jamal bet?
qa.a: She was probably worried and a little protective, holding his arm to save the cake-stall tokens.

grounding: A boy at a fair is sure black is due after a run of reds, believing the wheel balances itself.

passage: On the train home from school in Prague, Vera and Noa played cards for squares of chocolate. Vera had drawn no aces for nine rounds. "The next one's an ace," she said. "Nine rounds without. It's due." She bet four squares. Noa shuffled and dealt: a seven. "Okay, now it's even more due," Vera said, pushing in her last six squares. A queen. Noa laughed and broke a square in half to share. "You know the deck gets shuffled every time, right? It forgets." Vera frowned at the empty chocolate wrapper. "Then why does it feel like it owes me?" "Because you remember the nine rounds," Noa said. "The cards don't."

qa.q: How many rounds had Vera gone without an ace?
qa.a: Nine rounds.

qa.q: Why did Vera bet all her chocolate?

passage:
Dear Tushar,
You'll laugh. Remember our family's monsoon cricket pool, where everyone puts in ten rupees and picks a team? This year I picked the Rhinos, who had lost eight matches in a row. My reasoning was genius: they HAD to win soon. Eight losses meant a win was due. Dadu said, "Beta, they lost eight because their captain retired," but I didn't listen. I even talked Mishti into picking them with me.
They lost the next three. Mishti hasn't forgiven me.
When I told my maths teacher, she said each match is decided by the players on the day, not by what happened before. Streaks feel like they must end, she said, but they don't owe anybody anything.
Lesson learned. Next year I'm picking by who's actually playing.
Usha

qa.q: Why did the Rhinos lose eight, according to Dadu?
qa.a: Because their captain retired.

qa.q: Why was Usha sure the Rhinos would win soon?
qa.a: Usha felt confident that eight losses meant a win was due, as if the streak had to balance out.

qa.q: What does Usha plan for next year, and why is it better?
qa.a: Picking by who is actually playing, because matches depend on the players on the day, not on past streaks.

qa.q: How does Mishti feel about the pool?
qa.a: Mishti hasn't forgiven Usha for talking her into the Rhinos, so she is probably annoyed.

passage:
Dear Ganga,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me. You know the card app I started playing in April, just for fun? I've lost about thirty thousand rupees. It started small. Then I had a bad week, and I kept thinking, after this many losses a win is due; the app can't keep beating me. So I played more, and bigger, to catch the win when it came. It never came the way I thought.
Last night I sat on the hostel stairs until 3 a.m. and realised the cards don't know I've been losing. Each hand is new.
This morning I told Didi everything. She's coming on Saturday, and we have an appointment with the college counsellor on Monday. I've deleted the app.
Can you call me tonight? I don't want to be alone with this.
Nandini

passage: Minakshi, thanks for having me. I'm Sarita, and two years ago I was betting on cricket matches through an app on my phone. At first it was small. Then I lost five bets in a row, and something in my head said, "The next one's yours. It's due." So I bet bigger. And lost. And bet bigger again. Every loss made me more sure the win was coming, as if the universe kept a scoreboard. It doesn't. Each match is just a match. By the time I understood, I'd lost my semester fees. What stopped me was my roommate finding me crying over my phone at 2 a.m. She didn't lecture me. She sat with me and called a gambling helpline on speaker, right then. Now I help run a support group on campus. The win was never due. Help was.

Week one. Ira downloaded a colour-prediction game a hostel friend swore by: guess red or green, win double. She lost the first four rounds, then won one. "See, it balances," she told Naveen. He shrugged.
Week three. Ira had lost her mess money for the month. Red had come up seven times in a row the night before, so she put everything on green. Red again. "It's due," she kept whispering. "It has to switch." She skipped dinner to keep playing.
Week five. Naveen found her in the library, not studying, just staring at the screen, eyes red. "How much?" She told him. He didn't say "I told you." He walked with her that evening to the student welfare office, where the counsellor stayed late to talk with her and helped her block the app. Walking back, Ira said quietly, "Red didn't owe me anything."

passage: In the small market town, Pema noticed the change in Dorjee before anyone else. Her old school friend used to spend evenings fixing phones in his tiny shop. Now he spent them at the number-betting counter by the bus stand, notebook in hand. "Lost three days running," he told her on Friday, grinning too wide. "So tomorrow's mine. Luck has to turn." The next week he had borrowed from Avni, and the shop was shut on a weekday. Pema didn't give him a talk about odds. She sat with him on the shop step and said, "Dorjee, I'm worried about you. You're betting more every time you lose, and you're borrowing. I care about you too much to pretend I haven't noticed." He looked away. She added, "There's a counsellor at the district hospital who helps with this. I'll go with you on Monday."

Our company has a free, confidential counselling line. Would you call it? I'll sit with you in the conference room tomorrow if you want." He looked at the floor, then said, "Tomorrow."
